newsitem.title: USA: Morgan Stanley stokes USG spot gasoline price.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Stanley stokes USG spot gasoline price.

text.p: U.S. Gulf Coast spot gasoline prices soared recently as white-shoe Wall Street trading house Morgan Stanley was seen buying wet barrels to buttress the fate of a paper swap position, traders said Wednesday.
The New York-based trading house bought several 25,000 barrel parcels of gasoline in the last week to support prices as part of a broader strategy, traders said.
Morgan Stanley could not be reached for comment.
"The presumption is that they're buying little pieces of gasoline to help another deal they're pricing off a Platt's basis," a trader in Houston said.

It was not immediately clear what swap position or positions Morgan Stanley held in paper markets, but cash gasoline traders said the lengths to which the company was willing to buy, suggests its paper involvements were large.
"They are probably losing something on the cash side, but they're a lot longer on the paper," said on trader in Texas.
Swaps are custom-made financial instruments used for speculation or hedging financial risks, and it was widely believed Morgan Stanley was using swaps to speculate.

"In order for them to be paying up this much they would have to have a huge position," said another trader, noting the company has bought more than 250,000 barrels of "M4" regular conventional unleaded in Houston over the last week.

Other traders said the Wall Street firm bought as many as 300,000 barrels on Monday alone, when deals were heard done at levels as high as 5.50 cents over NYMEX gasoline futures for December delivery -- about 3.00 cents higher than differentials at the start of the day.
The price of "M4" for prompt delivery has risen by nearly three percent in the last week to nearly 68.00 cents a gallon tracking both NYMEX futures and firmer differentials.
Traders noted Morgan Stanley's buying has been done later in the day, often during the aftermarket, when an oil pricing service establishes quotes against which deals are priced.

Indeed, the cash market strength in Houston this week has pulled flagging gasoline futures on the NYMEX off their lows, with the firm cash differentials easily offsetting losses or outpacing gains on Monday and Tuesday respectively.
But traders also noted that while Morgan Stanley has been, and is likely to be a presence through November, a host of other factors have kept prices firm as well.

"I don't think (Morgan Stanley) is the whole story by any stretch of the imagination," said the Houston trader, noting lower inventories, refinery mishaps and planned maintenance projects this autumn, have kept the market much firmer than a year ago.
"They're getting away with it because there's some fundamental strength down in Houston. There's still a lot of refiner buying," another trader said.

Traders also noted that on Monday, the day of the sharpest price move in some time, the back 32nd cycle for scheduling shipments in the huge Houston-to-New York Colonial Pipeline expired, creating a rush to nominate barrels on the line.

Also, traders note the American Petroleum Institute's (API) annual meeting in Washington, D.C. earlier this week has kept just enough traders out of the market to make Morgan Stanley's task of raising prices that much easier.
